title: Berkshire 2013 letter: Invest like you own a farm, ignore the macro chatter
summary: Buffett's 2013 letter explains float, GEICO's cost-advantage moat, and Berkshire's flexible capital allocation. Its centerpiece is a lesson on investing: buy productive assets using future earnings, ignore market noise and price swings, and use a low-cost index fund if you are not an expert.

principles.text: Judge an asset by its future productivity, not by expected price changes; the latter is speculation.
principles.quote: Focus on the future productivity of the asset you are considering. If you don’t feel comfortable making a rough estimate of the asset’s future earnings, just forget it and move on.

principles.text: Focus on what the asset produces, not on daily price quotes.
principles.quote: Games are won by players who focus on the playing field – not by those whose eyes are glued to the scoreboard. If you can enjoy Saturdays and Sundays without looking at stock prices, give it a try on weekdays.

principles.text: Macro opinions and market predictions are a waste of time and can blur the facts that matter.
principles.quote: Forming macro opinions or listening to the macro or market predictions of others is a waste of time. Indeed, it is dangerous because it may blur your vision of the facts that are truly important.

principles.text: Fear is an opportunity for investors with cash; euphoria is the enemy.
principles.quote: A climate of fear is your friend when investing; a euphoric world is your enemy.

principles.text: Non-experts should own a low-cost S&P 500 index fund rather than try to pick winners.
principles.quote: The goal of the non-professional should not be to pick winners – neither he nor his “helpers” can do that – but should rather be to own a cross-section of businesses that in aggregate are bound to do well. A low-cost S&P 500 index fund will achieve this goal.

principles.text: A low-cost operation creates an enduring moat, as GEICO shows.
principles.quote: GEICO’s cost advantage is the factor that has enabled the company to gobble up market share year after year. Its low costs create a moat – an enduring one – that competitors are unable to cross.
